title: Anand Sahib: the song of bliss
hookLine: forty pauris of joy found through the Guru, closing every Sikh gathering

lines: ANAND KARAJ: THE CEREMONY OF BLISS.
cards: At a Sikh wedding, the couple walks slowly around the Guru Granth Sahib four times while the four verses called the Laavan are sung. Then the music shifts.
Before the final prayer, the whole room joins in a song: grandparents, cousins, friends who flew in, kids who've been fidgeting for an hour.
The same song closes the ordinary Sunday service, a baby's naming, and a funeral. And the wedding shares its first word: the ceremony is called Anand Karaj, the ceremony of bliss.

teach.b: Anand means bliss, a deep, settled joy.

teach.h: FORTY PAURIS; SIX CLOSE EVERY GATHERING.
teach.b: Anand Sahib is a bani by Guru Amar Das, the third Guru, in Raag Ramkali, set in the Guru Granth Sahib: forty pauris, forty stanzas.
You first met it on day one hundred thirty-three; now comes the slow walk through it, the way the Japji and Chaupai went. Two forms matter.

Many Sikhs say all forty pauris in the morning, as one of the five banis of the Nitnem. And a short form, the first five pauris and the last, six in all, closes nearly every Sikh gathering, followed by the Ardas.

teach.h: BORN, TRADITION SAYS, OF A FAMILY'S JOY.
teach.b: Sikh tradition tells that Guru Amar Das composed it when a grandson was born to his family, and the child was named Anand. Whether or not every detail is exact, the story fits: this song comes out of a family's joy.
And it's rarely a solo. It's the song a room sings. A wedding sings it on the way into a marriage; a funeral sings it on the way through grief.
The same words, in both rooms. That says something about anand in this tradition. It isn't the high of a good day.

teach.h: SUNG AT WEDDINGS AND FUNERALS ALIKE.
teach.b: It's a joy deep enough to be sung beside a coffin as well as beside a bride, a joy that can hold sorrow without breaking.
And it's found, the song will say, through the Guru.

how: Many Sikhs recite all forty pauris of Anand Sahib in the morning Nitnem, and the first five pauris with the fortieth are sung at the close of nearly every Sikh service and ceremony, before the Ardas.

o: a deep, settled joy that can hold sorrow
peace that comes only after you die
a passing thrill after a lucky day

games.q: the song of bliss — tap the pairs.
p: the third Guru, who wrote it
the first five and the fortieth

s: Anand Sahib is sung only at happy occasions
the same six pauris close weddings and funerals alike: a joy that can hold sorrow.
the Sikh wedding ceremony is called Anand Karaj, the ceremony of bliss
and the short Anand Sahib is sung near its close.
it has forty; six of them form the short version sung at every gathering.

games.q: it's the end of a Sikh service, and the whole room is about to sing. which song closes nearly every Sikh gathering before the Ardas?
o: the six pauris of Anand Sahib.
games.why: the first five pauris of Anand Sahib and the fortieth are sung together, then everyone stands for the Ardas.

practice: If you can, play a recording of the short Anand Sahib, the six pauris sung at the close of a Sikh service; it takes only a few minutes. Don't work at the words yet; just breathe with the sound of many voices singing one thing.
If you can't play it now, picture a room full of people you love singing together, and if you pray, join with Waheguru at the end.

wordCard.voice: Anand. Bliss, a deep and settled joy; Guru Amar Das's forty-pauri song, whose six pauris close nearly every Sikh gathering, weddings and funerals alike.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: anand, bliss; the name of Guru Amar Das's song of forty pauris in Raag Ramkali.

carryVoice: Your line: bliss, together. Six pauris, many voices, and one song between them. Day three hundred eighty.
